analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices and offer a government-run drug plan.
analysis.headline: The bill to let Medicare negotiate drug prices was sent to two House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the 'noninterference' rule that has barred Medicare from negotiating drug prices since the Medicare drug benefit was created in 2003 [S3]. It directs the President to negotiate prices with drug manufacturers for everyone enrolled in a Medicare drug plan, publish the results in reports to Congress every six months, and offer a government-run Medicare drug plan that uses negotiated prices and a formulary steering patients toward drugs with the best value [S3] [S2]. An advisory committee of physicians, pharmacists, and consumers would review clinical evidence to decide which drugs belong on that formulary [S3]. It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to their Health subcommittees, and never advanced [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — roughly 40 million older and disabled Americans — would pay less for prescription drugs if the government used its buying power to negotiate lower prices than the private drug plans pay today [S3]. All drug plans would benefit from the negotiated prices too, so some savings could flow to everyone's premiums and copays, not just users of the new public plan [S3]. Taxpayers would gain as well, since Medicare subsidizes part of the drug benefit for low-income beneficiaries.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the 2003 'noninterference' provision that expressly prohibits the government from negotiating Part D drug prices, and instead requires the President to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with drug manufacturers for covered Part D drugs [S3].
Creates a Medicare-operated prescription drug plan offered nationwide, which would buy drugs at the negotiated prices and compete with private plans, with a nationally uniform premium [S3].

Requires a formulary built on clinical-evidence assessments by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, with incentives to steer patients to drugs that cost less and work as well or better, and lets the plan waive cost-sharing when that would improve adherence and reduce hospital costs [S3].
Requires the President to report to Congress every six months on the negotiations and the prices and discounts achieved [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would see revenue fall from the negotiated prices and rebates, and from a formulary that steers patients to cheaper equivalents. Private drug plan and Medicare Advantage insurers would face a new government-run competitor for enrollment. Pharmaceutical companies argue that lower prices reduce the revenue that funds research into new medicines.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and private drug plans

drawbacks.text: The bill hands negotiation authority to a single person — the President — rather than a professional agency, an unusual design the bill's own findings connect to the sitting President's self-description as a 'master negotiator' [S3]. A future administration could negotiate differently or not at all, making savings unstable.

Formulary incentives such as prior authorization, step therapy, and reference pricing can delay or restrict access to specific drugs for some patients, even though the bill requires the formulary to preserve medically necessary access and allows additions for new treatment options [S3].

Reduced drug revenue could mean less industry spending on developing new medicines, the standard objection to government price negotiation; the bill contains no offsetting mechanism to preserve research incentives.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential savings for beneficiaries are large, since Medicare drug prices in the United States run well above what other governments and large private purchasers pay, and the bill keeps private plans in place rather than replacing them. The main design weaknesses are real but narrow: concentrating negotiation in the President personally is unconventional and makes the policy hostage to whoever holds the office, and a value-based formulary can burden some patients with access hurdles. On balance the cost side falls mostly on drug manufacturers, which is exactly the tradeoff the bill intends.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees, then to their Health subcommittees, and died there without a hearing or a vote when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5] [S1].

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on March 29, 2017, with Rep. John Conyers among its two cosponsors [S3] [S4].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced [S5].

In late March and early April 2017 it was referred to the Health subcommittee of each committee, the lowest procedural rung, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because the 2003 rule barring Medicare from negotiating prices — and protecting their Part D pricing — remained in place. Private drug plans also avoided a government-run competitor. For the 40 million or so Medicare beneficiaries, drug prices continued to be set without government negotiation.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported it, and with Republicans holding the House majority the bill was never scheduled for action.

industries.note: The bill repeals the noninterference rule that keeps the government out of price negotiation and requires negotiated prices, discounts, and rebates for Medicare drugs, directly cutting into manufacturer revenue. Its gain is the public's savings.

industries.industry: Private Medicare Part D drug plans and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: A Medicare-operated plan offered nationwide would compete with private plans for enrollment, but the negotiated prices would also apply to what private plans pay for drugs, lowering their purchase costs. Their resistance to a public competitor runs against beneficiaries' interest in cheaper drugs.
The bill's formulary encourages generic substitution and competitive bidding for drugs with similar clinical benefit, directing more sales toward cheaper generic alternatives.
